problem: The area of a square increases at a rate of $4{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the lengths of the sides of the square increasing when the sides are $1\text{ m}$ long?

feedback.problem: The area of a square decreases at a rate of $40{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the lengths of the sides of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\text{ m}$ long?
feedback.worked_solution:
Here, the area is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/d410da34cd3c90570266b32351b41560f804f8c04be77e9089414a5cf374909b.png)

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-40\text{ m}{}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-40 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{20}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when the sides are $10\,\text{m},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{20}{10}=-2.
$$

Therefore, the lengths of the sides are decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s}.$
